claims.text: Resistance to simultaneous wear and corrosion in high-entropy alloys is governed by the formation of a stable passive oxide layer.
Alloying elements influence passive oxide-layer formation and stability.
Microstructure influences passive oxide-layer formation and stability.
Mechanical properties influence passive oxide-layer formation and stability.
Chromium, molybdenum, or titanium additions can be used to alter the behavior of the high-entropy alloy.
The proposed governing structural mediator is passive oxide-layer formation and stability.
A stable passive oxide layer reduces contact between the alloy surface and the corrosive environment.
Reduced contact between the alloy surface and the corrosive environment reduces corrosion.
Reduced contact between the alloy surface and the corrosive environment reduces wear.
High-entropy alloys with optimized alloying-element compositions will have better simultaneous wear-corrosion resistance than the baseline alloy.
Optimized alloys will have a lower wear rate than the baseline alloy.
Optimized alloys will have a lower corrosion rate than the baseline alloy.
The prediction may fail for alloys that deviate significantly from typical high-entropy-alloy composition or microstructure.
The exact mechanisms by which alloying elements affect passive oxide-layer formation and stability are not fully understood.
